paragraphs: Paying an AI provider according to output quality creates an evaluation problem: noisy assessments increase expected payments, but more elaborate assessments cost money themselves. The paper studies how an organization can balance these costs when delegating text generation. Its central idea is to make the evaluation process adaptive, using an initial coarse signal to decide whether a more detailed assessment is worth performing.

The authors develop algorithms for finding optimal adaptive contracts when natural assumptions hold or when the main problem dimensions are small. They also prove that approximating the optimum is hard in the general unstructured setting. This distinguishes cases where selective evaluation can be optimized efficiently from cases where designing the contract itself becomes computationally difficult.

The work additionally considers randomized versions of adaptive contracts and examines their benefits and limitations. Experiments using question-answering and code-generation datasets demonstrate advantages over non-adaptive baselines. The stated contribution is therefore both economic and computational: selective evaluation can improve delegation efficiency, while the theory identifies conditions under which suitable contracts can be computed.
icml-2026-adaptive-contracts-for-cost-ef.tldr: Adaptive contracts selectively request detailed evaluations to improve the cost efficiency of delegating text generation to AI providers.

paragraphs: Diffusion models can generate rich outputs, but the internal representations used for generation are not explicitly arranged around interpretable controls. ConDA adds a geometry layer to a pretrained model, using contrastive learning and auxiliary information such as time, stimulation settings, or facial action units. It learns a smaller representation whose directions align with factors governing how the underlying system changes.

Editing happens in this smaller space, where nonlinear paths support smooth transitions, extrapolation, and counterfactual changes. A decoder based on nearby examples maps those paths back into the original diffusion representation while preserving neighborhood relationships. The original diffusion space remains responsible for rendering, separating the organization of controls from the generation process itself.

The authors evaluate this approach across fluid dynamics, biological imaging and activity, neurostimulation, and facial expressions. They report more interpretable and controllable representations than linear traversals and conditioning-based baselines, together with robustness across inversion solvers. These findings indicate that pretrained diffusion representations contain useful dynamical structure that an explicit contrastive geometry layer can expose for editing.
icml-2026-contrastive-diffusion-alignmen.tldr: ConDA organizes pretrained diffusion representations into a smaller, interpretable space for controlling generation along meaningful dynamical directions.

paragraphs: Late-interaction retrieval systems store multiple token vectors per document, making their indexes expensive. Compressing each vector to minimize reconstruction error can miss what matters for ranking: a small set of winning token matches may determine a document's score. CrossQ instead makes compression sensitive to document context and trains it to preserve retrieval behavior.

Its token codes depend on lightweight context computed during indexing, without storing that context. Training objectives preserve candidate score distributions and protect score margins against hard negatives. At two bytes per token, CrossQ improves MRR@10 by 0.010 over the strongest strictly footprint-matched quantization baseline and by 0.012 over the strongest candidate-matched system reference.

At four bytes per token, it improves average nDCG@10 by 0.009 on the reported nine-dataset BEIR subset. Storage reduction is 64-fold for raw tokens, approximately 61-fold with metadata, and approximately 58-fold with conservative padding and alignment. At eight bytes per token, light fine-tuning retains approximately 98% of full-precision ColBERT MRR@10. These results show how ranking-aware compression can improve the trade-off between index size and retrieval quality.
icml-2026-crossq-task-aligned-cross-toke.tldr: CrossQ compresses retrieval token vectors using document context and ranking-aware training to improve quality at small index sizes.

paragraphs: Masked diffusion language models offer parallel, controllable generation, but the abstract identifies two disadvantages relative to autoregressive models: worse perplexity and missing inference optimizations, especially key-value caching. Eso-LMs connect these model families through any-order autoregression, creating a family that smoothly interpolates between their perplexities while retaining useful generation capabilities.

The architectural change is to use causal attention rather than the bidirectional attention typically employed by masked diffusion denoisers. By exploiting the connection to any-order autoregressive models, the authors make exact likelihood computation possible for masked diffusion models. They also enable exact key-value caching, allowing previously computed attention information to be reused while preserving parallel generation across the full sequence length.

Combined with an optimized sampling schedule, this design establishes a new reported state of the art on the speed-quality frontier for unconditional generation. The contribution joins tractable probability evaluation with an inference efficiency mechanism that masked diffusion had lacked. The stated performance result concerns the balance between generation speed and quality, making both aspects central to assessing the model family.
icml-2026-esoteric-language-models-a-fam.tldr: Eso-LMs combine autoregressive and masked diffusion ideas to enable exact likelihoods, exact key-value caching, and efficient parallel generation.

paragraphs: Evolution Strategies optimize objectives by evaluating parameter perturbations, making them applicable to noisy or non-differentiable problems. Although these evaluations can run in parallel, unstructured random perturbations make large GPU workloads inefficient. EGGROLL addresses this computational bottleneck by expressing individual perturbations as low-rank matrices, increasing the useful arithmetic performed by the resulting batched operations.

For billion-parameter models with large populations, the authors report a hundredfold training speed increase and throughput reaching up to 91% of pure batch inference. Their theoretical analysis examines conditions for Evolution Strategies updates to converge in high dimensions, identifies a linearizing effect, and establishes consistency between EGGROLL and Evolution Strategies as parameter dimension increases.

Experiments demonstrate stable pretraining of nonlinear recurrent language models operating entirely with integer datatypes. They also find EGGROLL competitive with GRPO for reasoning-oriented language-model post-training and report no performance compromise relative to Evolution Strategies in reinforcement learning from scratch. Together, these findings suggest that structured perturbations can substantially improve execution efficiency while retaining useful optimization behavior in the studied settings.
icml-2026-evolution-strategies-at-the-hy.tldr: EGGROLL uses low-rank perturbations to make large-scale Evolution Strategies substantially faster while preserving performance in the reported experiments.

paragraphs: A deployed classifier may need different balances between fairness and accuracy as requirements change. Methods that adjust predictions after training offer this flexibility, but can lose substantial accuracy. Methods that incorporate fairness during training can produce better trade-offs, yet changing the desired balance typically requires expensive retraining. This paper aims to combine flexible adjustment with an efficient fairness-accuracy trade-off.

The proposed algorithm learns feature representations specifically to improve the behavior of post-processing fair classifiers. It uses gradient-based optimization to shape the information available to the later adjustment stage. The key design choice is therefore to prepare the representation during training so that changing the fairness-accuracy balance afterward can work more effectively.

Experiments on real-world datasets show trade-off efficiency comparable to, and sometimes better than, the in-processing methods considered. These adjustments do not require retraining the proposed model. The findings support a practical connection between representation learning and deployment flexibility: training can improve the options available to a later fairness adjustment, rather than committing the model to a single balance.
icml-2026-fair-classification-with-effic.tldr: Learning representations for post-processing lets classifiers adjust their fairness-accuracy balance after training while achieving competitive trade-off efficiency.

paragraphs: Autoregressive video diffusion generates video incrementally, but its attention cache expands as generation continues. This increases latency and GPU memory use, limiting the temporal context available for consistent long videos. FAST-AR targets three observed redundancies: similar cached keys across frames, slowly changing semantic attention information, and long prompts with only a few relevant tokens for each frame.

The framework combines three training-free components. TempCache compresses cached keys and values using temporal correspondence to bound cache growth. AnnCA uses approximate nearest-neighbor matching to select prompt tokens relevant to a frame. AnnSA applies a similar matching approach within self-attention, restricting each query to semantically related keys. Together, these components reduce storage and attention computation in existing autoregressive diffusion backbones and world models.

Experiments report end-to-end speedups reaching five- to tenfold while maintaining near-identical visual quality. Long rollouts retain stable throughput and nearly constant peak GPU memory, whereas prior methods progressively slow and consume more memory. The findings make sustained generation efficiency a central result alongside faster individual computations.
icml-2026-fast-ar-fast-autoregressive-vi.tldr: FAST-AR combines temporal cache compression and sparse attention to accelerate video diffusion while stabilizing memory use and throughput during long generation.

paragraphs: Evaluating generated samples often involves representing real and generated data in a high-dimensional space and measuring distances between them. The paper shows that these representations suffer from hubness, which distorts nearest-neighbor relationships. Because distance-based evaluation depends on those relationships, this distortion can bias the metrics used to assess a generative model.

The authors introduce Generative Iterative Contextual Dissimilarity Measure, or GICDM, building on an existing contextual dissimilarity method. GICDM corrects neighborhood estimation for both real and generated samples. The work also adds a multi-scale extension to improve empirical behavior. Its point of intervention is the geometry used for evaluation: it changes how sample relationships are estimated before those relationships inform assessments of generation quality.

Experiments on synthetic and real benchmarks show that GICDM resolves failures caused by hubness, restores reliable metric behavior, and improves agreement with human assessment. These findings connect a geometric defect in the representation space to practical evaluation errors. Correcting that defect can make distance-based assessments better reflect the quality that evaluators intend to measure.
icml-2026-gicdm-mitigating-hubness-for-r.tldr: GICDM corrects hubness-distorted neighborhoods to improve the reliability and human alignment of distance-based generative-model evaluation.

paragraphs: This paper asks when having many dimensions helps reveal structure in data. It distinguishes effective dimension, which measures variability across feature directions; correlation rank, which measures functional complexity across samples; and latent intrinsic dimension, which describes the hidden manifold. Separating these quantities clarifies why a large feature space need not imply equally complex underlying structure.

Within a general random function model, the authors show that increasing effective dimension makes data dot products concentrate around their expected values. Under continuity assumptions ensuring that added features provide additional information, persistence diagrams recover latent homology when effective dimension grows faster than the logarithm of the sample count. Thus, the beneficial result depends on informative dimension growth and the stated assumptions.

The authors also revisit evidence of toroidal structure in grid-cell activity. Their analysis provides the first reported empirical evidence that this structure is isometric to a flat torus model of physical space. This suggests a geometrically faithful representation, extending the interpretation beyond identifying a toroidal topological shape.
icml-2026-how-high-is-high-rethinking-th.tldr: The paper distinguishes three dimensions of data and shows conditions under which increasing effective dimension helps recover hidden geometric structure.

paragraphs: FlowOptimizer learns how to move a population of candidate solutions toward better objective values. Each optimization step is represented by a velocity field that uses information about the candidates, including their values, gradients, and population statistics. This lets the learned update depend on both individual candidates and the broader state of the search.

Training begins by matching displacements between source populations and improved target populations obtained through sampling, without simulating the full optimization process. The model is then unfolded across multiple iterations, and the entire sequence is fine-tuned directly against objective values for a targeted problem class. This self-supervised approach does not require known solutions as training targets.

Evaluations cover non-convex benchmarks and applications in robotics, power grids, and supply chains. The authors report improvements of orders of magnitude in solution quality over established traditional and learned optimization methods. They also demonstrate training on lower-dimensional problems followed by successful generalization to problems with ten times as many dimensions. These results support learning coordinated search updates from objective-based feedback.
icml-2026-learning-to-optimize-via-deep-.tldr: FlowOptimizer learns population-based optimization steps through flow models, achieving large reported solution-quality gains without needing known optimal solutions.

paragraphs: Speculative decoding speeds up language generation by letting a small model propose tokens that a larger target model verifies in parallel. Its effectiveness depends strongly on how many proposed tokens are accepted. Draft models are commonly trained using Kullback-Leibler divergence, but this objective only serves as a proxy for the acceptance behavior that determines useful progress.

The paper explains why the proxy can fall short: KL divergence and acceptance rate share a global optimum, yet small draft models have limited capacity and usually reach suboptimal solutions. At those solutions, reducing KL divergence need not maximize acceptance. LK losses directly target acceptance rate, aligning training more closely with the draft model's role during generation.

Experiments span four draft architectures and six target models ranging from 8 billion to 685 billion parameters. Acceptance metrics improve across all tested configurations, with reported average acceptance-length gains reaching 8–10% across general, coding, and math evaluations. The authors describe the losses as easy to implement, free of additional computational overhead, and compatible with existing speculator training frameworks.
icml-2026-lk-losses-direct-acceptance-ra.tldr: LK losses train speculative draft models directly for token acceptance, improving acceptance metrics over KL-based training in every tested configuration.

paragraphs: A pretrained diffusion model may generate convincing samples whose characteristics still differ from a user's reference data. Adapting the model is especially challenging when only a few examples are available and retraining is infeasible. MMD Guidance addresses this setting by changing the sampling process using a direct measure of distributional mismatch.

The method adds gradients of Maximum Mean Discrepancy between generated samples and a reference dataset to reverse diffusion. This steers generation toward the reference distribution. The authors motivate MMD through its estimation behavior with limited data, low observed variance, and efficient differentiability. These properties make it suitable for repeatedly guiding samples during generation.

The framework extends to prompt-aware conditional generation through product kernels and can operate efficiently inside the latent space of latent diffusion models. Experiments on synthetic and real-world benchmarks show that it can improve distributional alignment while preserving sample fidelity. The stated result is that adaptation can happen at inference time, with the reference dataset influencing generation without requiring additional model training.
icml-2026-mmd-guidance-training-free-dis.tldr: MMD Guidance adapts diffusion sampling toward a reference distribution without retraining, with experiments showing alignment gains while preserving sample fidelity.

paragraphs: Minimum Bayes Risk decoding chooses a generated candidate by assessing its expected utility against sampled pseudo-references. The paper examines a directional mismatch in this procedure: commonly used evaluation metrics, including BLEU and COMET, are asymmetric. Comparing a candidate with a reference can therefore behave differently from comparing the same pair with their roles reversed.

The authors introduce a noisy-channel decomposition that incorporates both directions. It separates the decision into candidate-to-reference likelihood, reference-to-candidate likelihood, a candidate prior, and a reference prior. By identifying these four contributions, the framework gives a unified interpretation of existing MBR variants and makes it possible to examine what each channel contributes for a particular metric and task.

The analysis finds that channel contributions differ across metrics while showing consistency across tasks. This suggests that metric choice affects how the two directions and priors influence selection. The results also suggest that weighting channels appropriately may improve on original MBR decoding. That improvement remains a qualified implication of the analysis, rather than a universal claim about every weighting or application.
icml-2026-noisy-channel-minimum-bayes-ri.tldr: A noisy-channel decomposition exposes directional effects in MBR decoding and suggests that appropriate channel weighting may improve candidate selection.

paragraphs: Online structured prediction makes label predictions sequentially as inputs arrive. Existing surrogate-regret guarantees compare performance with a single fixed estimator, but that reference can become poor when the environment changes. Even a bounded excess over its surrogate loss may offer little reassurance if the reference loss itself grows linearly with time.

The paper instead compares cumulative target loss with a sequence of estimators that can change. Its bound is F_T + O(1 + P_T), where F_T is that sequence's cumulative surrogate loss and P_T measures how far it moves. Time enters only through these two quantities, connecting performance to how well a changing reference predicts and how much adaptation it requires.

The approach combines dynamic regret analysis for online gradient descent with a technique that exploits the gap between target and surrogate losses. It explains the usefulness of a Polyak-style learning rate, which also performs well empirically, and extends the framework using convolutional Fenchel–Young loss. A matching lower-bound result shows that the dependence on F_T and P_T is tight.
icml-2026-non-stationary-online-structur.tldr: The paper bounds online prediction loss against a changing comparator, with tight dependence on its surrogate loss and amount of movement.

paragraphs: Normalization equivariance requires an image-processing function to respond predictably when its input is multiplied by a positive scale and shifted by a constant: the output must undergo the same transformation. Existing ways of enforcing this property constrain every internal layer. Those constraints add runtime cost and exclude standard transformer operations such as softmax attention and LayerNorm.

Wrapped Normalization Equivariance uses a parameter-free outer wrapper instead. It normalizes the input, runs a chosen backbone, and then denormalizes the output. The authors prove that every normalization-equivariant function can be expressed in this form. Consequently, the factorization exactly describes the desired function class while allowing the backbone to use ordinary architectural components.

In blind image denoising experiments, wrapping both convolutional and transformer architectures improves robustness when noise levels differ from those expected by the model. The wrapper has no measurable GPU overhead in the reported evaluation, whereas architectural equivariance baselines are up to 1.6 times slower. The result makes this structural robustness property accessible without imposing restrictions throughout the network.
icml-2026-normalization-equivariance-for.tldr: A parameter-free normalization wrapper enforces normalization equivariance for arbitrary backbones and improves denoising robustness without measurable GPU overhead.

paragraphs: Momentum combines gradient information over time, but old information can become misleading when the optimum moves. This paper analyzes stochastic gradient descent and its Polyak Heavy-Ball and Nesterov momentum variants in that tracking setting. The analysis assumes strongly convex, smooth objectives, making the question precise within a defined class of changing optimization problems.

Finite-time bounds divide tracking error into three parts: the transient effect of initialization, the contribution of stochastic noise, and the contribution of optimum drift. This exposes a specific cost of momentum under distribution shift. Its drift-amplification penalty diverges as the momentum parameter approaches one, producing systematic lag because the update continues to average stale gradients.

Lower bounds under gradient-variation constraints show that this penalty reflects a genuine information-theoretic barrier rather than looseness in the upper-bound analysis. In drift-dominated regimes, momentum is provably worse. The paper identifies regime boundaries where ordinary SGD outperforms its accelerated counterparts, providing a theoretical explanation for instability observed with momentum in dynamic settings without claiming that momentum is inferior in every regime.
icml-2026-on-the-provable-suboptimality-.tldr: Under strong convexity and smoothness, momentum provably amplifies tracking lag enough for ordinary SGD to outperform it in drift-dominated regimes.

paragraphs: Recovering a dynamical system from stationary snapshots is difficult because those measurements do not directly show change over time. The paper studies multivariate Ornstein–Uhlenbeck processes using observational snapshots together with interventions. This setting fits applications such as gene perturbation experiments, where complete time-series trajectories may be unavailable.

The main theorem gives a sufficient intervention pattern: one intervention per strongly connected component of the drift graph generically identifies all process parameters up to a global scaling factor. It requires a connected component-condensation graph with a single root and spectral nondegeneracy assumptions. These qualifications specify when the intervention count supports recovery and what ambiguity remains.

The authors construct a recursive algorithm that processes components in topological order, isolates their marginal dynamics, and solves linear equations using already recovered upstream parameters. They also propose regularized least squares that jointly fits steady-state mean and covariance equations across observational and interventional data. Synthetic and real-data experiments demonstrate effective parameter recovery and prediction of unseen interventions, connecting the identifiability result to an estimation procedure.
icml-2026-one-intervention-per-component.tldr: Under stated graph and spectral conditions, one intervention per strongly connected component generically identifies linear stochastic dynamics up to global scale.

paragraphs: Some peer-review policies allow language models to polish human-written reviews while prohibiting broader use. Enforcing that distinction requires identifying how a review was produced, including mixed human-AI workflows. The authors assemble a dataset simulating different degrees of collaboration and test five leading AI-text detectors, including two commercial systems.

Every tested detector labels a non-trivial fraction of permitted, LLM-polished reviews as AI-generated. This creates a risk of accusing reviewers of misconduct for assistance that the policies allow. The authors also examine whether access to the submitted manuscript and the specialized nature of scientific writing can improve detection. These signals produce measurable gains in some settings, but none of the investigated approaches reaches the accuracy standard required for this use.

The findings also affect estimates of AI use across peer review. Detectors can treat collaborative reviews as fully AI-generated, potentially inflating estimates of policy violations. The paper therefore questions enforcement through current detection methods and urges caution when interpreting public estimates based on those methods.
icml-2026-policies-permitting-llm-use-fo.tldr: Tested AI-text detectors cannot reliably distinguish permitted review polishing from prohibited generation, risking false accusations and inflated violation estimates.

paragraphs: Adaptive experiments can collect expensive labeled outcomes while also having access to abundant unlabeled data and AI predictions. Using those predictions for statistical inference is challenging because they may be inaccurate, and adaptive data collection violates the independent, identically distributed setting of classical methods. PPAI combines these information sources in a single estimating equation.

The authors establish asymptotic normality under mild conditions on the data-collection policy, supporting confidence intervals and hypothesis tests for a broad class of quantities described by estimating equations. A data-driven tuning mechanism adjusts the weight given to AI predictions according to how informative they are. This makes prediction usefulness part of the estimator's operation.

The resulting asymptotic variance is guaranteed to be no worse than that of a labeled-only baseline and strictly smaller when predictions are informative. Numerical experiments support efficiency gains with useful predictions and robustness when predictions are inaccurate. The guarantee concerns asymptotic inference under the stated policy conditions, providing a principled route for incorporating pretrained predictions into adaptive experimentation.
icml-2026-prediction-powered-adaptive-in.tldr: PPAI combines AI predictions with adaptive experiment data to improve asymptotic inference efficiency when predictions help, without worsening baseline asymptotic variance.

paragraphs: Post-training quantization rounds model values into a more compact representation, making large outliers troublesome. Block rotations spread these values before rounding with less overhead than full-vector rotations. This paper analyzes how the arrangement of values across blocks affects outlier suppression, showing that the input vector's geometry fundamentally limits what a block rotation can achieve.

In the deterministic worst case, post-rotation outliers are minimized when the input's absolute-value mass is evenly distributed across blocks. PeRQ uses this insight to permute activations before rotation and quantization. A greedy calibration algorithm balances expected blockwise mass. The authors identify transformer regions where these permutations can be folded into weights, avoiding extra inference overhead.

Experiments show accuracy improvements across every tested block size. For Llama3 1B quantized to INT4 with block size 16, the reported recovery relative to full-vector rotation perplexity reaches 90%, compared with 46% without permutations. The result connects a geometric analysis to a deployment-compatible adjustment: better placement of values lets inexpensive block rotations suppress outliers more effectively.
icml-2026-pushing-the-limits-of-block-ro.tldr: PeRQ redistributes activation mass before block rotation, improving post-training quantization accuracy without adding inference overhead.

paragraphs: Masked diffusion has become the dominant discrete diffusion approach to language modeling, helped by strong perplexity results. This paper broadens the comparison with the first reported scaling-law study of uniform-state and interpolating discrete diffusion methods. It also finds that a simple cross-entropy training objective makes masked diffusion approximately 12% more efficient in floating-point computation.

The main comparison separates likelihood performance from practical generation behavior. Perplexity is informative when comparing models within one diffusion family, but can mislead across families. A method with worse likelihood scaling may still offer a preferable combination of sampling speed and output quality. The authors therefore examine the speed-quality frontier alongside likelihood-based measurements.

Scaling all methods to 1.7 billion parameters, they find uniform-state diffusion competitive on likelihood benchmarks and better than the compared autoregressive and masked diffusion models on GSM8K, despite worse validation perplexity. These results challenge categorical preference for masked diffusion and show why a single language-modeling metric can overlook useful generation and task-performance advantages.
icml-2026-scaling-beyond-masked-diffusio.tldr: Scaling comparisons show that uniform-state diffusion can remain competitive and outperform masked diffusion on GSM8K despite worse validation perplexity.

paragraphs: Compressing a model below one bit per weight becomes difficult when weight magnitudes are heavily compressed but their positive or negative signs still require storage. Across Transformers, convolutional networks, and multilayer perceptrons, the authors find that learned sign matrices resist low-rank approximation. Their spectral behavior is indistinguishable from independent random signs, creating the compression barrier described as the one-bit wall.

Despite this apparent randomness, most weights keep the signs assigned at initialization. Sign changes mainly occur through rare crossings near zero, suggesting that much of the final sign-pattern randomness is inherited. The paper formalizes this mechanism through a stopping-time analysis of sign changes under stochastic gradient noise. With bounded updates and rare re-entry near zero, effective sign-flip counts have a geometric tail.

The authors then introduce training from scratch with a low-rank sign template to prevent this barrier from emerging. The approach connects a compression obstacle to training dynamics: if signs tend to persist, structuring them during training offers a way to avoid inheriting an expensive random pattern.
icml-2026-sign-lock-in-randomly-initiali.tldr: Persistent initialization signs help explain a sub-bit compression barrier, motivating training from scratch with low-rank sign templates.

paragraphs: Biomedical images vary with technical experimental conditions as well as biology. These batch effects can prevent a model from generalizing across experiments. The paper addresses a setting with multiple domains during both training and inference, where standard assumptions of one source and one target domain are insufficient. It also shows that existing normalization-based adaptation approaches degrade with small target batches and changing label distributions.

CS-ARM-BN uses negative control samples as stable context for adaptation. These controls are present across experimental batches and provide a basis for stabilizing domain statistics. The method incorporates them during both training and inference through a meta-learning approach to batch-normalization adaptation, directly addressing the instability of statistics derived from changing target batches.

Experiments evaluate mechanism-of-action classification on the large JUMP-CP imaging dataset, a task relevant to drug discovery. The authors report substantially improved robustness to batch-size changes and shifts in class distributions. The findings show how experimental controls can support model adaptation, helping separate technical variation from the biological differences the classifier is intended to recognize.
icml-2026-stabilizing-in-context-multi-s.tldr: CS-ARM-BN uses negative controls to stabilize biomedical image adaptation under small batches and shifting class distributions.

paragraphs: Correcting a reasoning failure requires identifying where it began. This paper studies whether language models can locate their own errors more reliably when reasoning is divided into discrete, coherent thoughts. The authors find that this structure improves error localization compared with conventional unstructured chain-of-thought reasoning, making the form of the reasoning process part of the correction method.

Their framework, Thought-ICS, generates one complete thought at a time, treating each as a deliberate decision with a clear boundary. After verification, the model identifies the first erroneous step. The system then returns to the last correct point and samples an alternative continuation. This organizes correction around a localized decision instead of treating the entire reasoning sequence as an undifferentiated object.

When an oracle has verified that reasoning is incorrect, Thought-ICS achieves a reported 20–40% self-correction lift. In a separate autonomous setting without external verification, it outperforms contemporary self-correction baselines. Keeping these settings distinct matters: the numerical lift is reported for oracle-verified errors, while the autonomous result establishes a comparative improvement without external verification.
icml-2026-structure-enables-effective-se.tldr: Structuring reasoning into complete thoughts improves error localization and supports correction by backtracking to the last correct step.

paragraphs: Sampling from complicated high-dimensional distributions is difficult when gradients are unavailable or too expensive to compute. The paper studies this black-box setting for non-log-concave distributions whose densities are known only up to normalization. It develops a zeroth-order Langevin method, using density evaluations to estimate the gradient information needed to guide sampling.

The proposed estimator reduces variance relative to the classical batched zeroth-order estimator and removes an unfavorable dependence of the required batch size on dimension. The authors establish the first reported non-asymptotic convergence guarantees for this sampling setting using relative Fisher information. They also obtain guarantees in squared total variation distance under a Poincaré inequality assumption, making that additional distributional condition explicit.

The work extends the method to ZO-APMC, a posterior sampler for black-box inverse problems using pretrained score-based generative priors, with corresponding non-asymptotic guarantees. Synthetic experiments validate the theory, while linear and nonlinear inverse-problem experiments show strong empirical performance. The contribution combines more stable gradient estimation with finite-run analysis and an application to recovering unknown quantities from observations.
icml-2026-zeroth-order-non-log-concave-s.tldr: A variance-reduced gradient-free Langevin sampler gains finite-run convergence guarantees and supports posterior sampling for black-box inverse problems.
